analysis.one_liner: Replaces flat farm subsidy checks with revenue-loss payments, expands crop insurance, and extends food assistance through 2017.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed this farm bill 64-35 on June 21, 2012, but the House never voted on it, and it never became law.
analysis.plain_summary: This five-year farm bill would end the best-known farm subsidy — direct payments sent to landowners whether or not they planted anything — and replace it with payments that kick in only when crop revenue falls below a guarantee. It expands federally subsidized crop insurance, replaces dairy price supports with a margin-insurance program, continues the sugar loan program, and extends SNAP (food stamps) and a long list of rural development, conservation, and research programs through 2017. The Senate passed it with a large bipartisan vote, but the House never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Commodity farmers get revenue-loss coverage and expanded crop insurance instead of unconditional checks; dairy farmers get margin protection; low-income households keep SNAP; rural residents get broadband, water, and energy-efficiency loan programs; beginning, veteran, and socially disadvantaged farmers get set-asides and premium breaks; anyone earning over $750,000 a year loses most subsidy eligibility.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farmers, SNAP recipients, and rural communities

how_it_helps.text: Ends direct payments, countercyclical payments, and the ACRE program, and replaces them with Agriculture Risk Coverage that pays producers only when actual crop revenue falls below 89% of a five-year benchmark revenue [S3][S4].
Prohibits farm commodity benefits for anyone whose average adjusted gross income exceeds $750,000 and cuts crop insurance premium subsidies by 15 percentage points for those above that income [S3].

Extends SNAP and other nutrition programs through FY2017, and adds rules like ending benefits for households with large lottery or gambling winnings and limiting eligibility for college students [S2][S3].

Repeals the dairy price support program and the milk income loss program and instead pays participating dairy operations whenever the production margin falls below $4 per hundredweight, with optional buy-up coverage [S3].

Continues disaster assistance for livestock losses from drought, fire, and weather; funds rural broadband grants, 911 expansion, water and waste systems, and 0% interest loans for home energy-efficiency upgrades [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the commodity, insurance, and conservation programs. Consumers continue to pay above-world-market prices for sugar under the loan program, and the new dairy supply-management program could tighten milk supplies and raise retail milk prices when margins are low. Food retailers bear the cost of electronic benefit transfer equipment for SNAP.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, plus consumers of sugar and possibly milk

drawbacks.text: Continues the sugar program — nonrecourse loans to cane and beet processors at fixed rates through 2017 — which in practice keeps domestic sugar prices above world prices, a cost embedded in the price of food [S3].

The new dairy market stabilization program can order reduced payments to high-production dairies when margins are low, a supply-restriction mechanism critics warned would raise milk prices for consumers [S3].

Much of the money 'saved' from direct payments is shifted into crop insurance, with new federal premium subsidies of 70% for a supplemental coverage option and 80% for a stacked income protection plan for cotton — subsidies that flow through private insurers and mostly benefit larger operations [S3].

The income test is loose by ordinary standards: a farmer with adjusted gross income up to $750,000 remains fully eligible for subsidies and only loses 15 points of insurance premium subsidy above that [S3].

Tightens SNAP on the margins — limiting college students to career and technical programs and ending benefits for households with substantial lottery or gambling winnings — while keeping overall eligibility intact [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill honestly ends the most criticized farm subsidy — unconditional checks to landowners — and adds a real income limit, which is genuine reform. But the savings are largely recycled into crop insurance premium subsidies that flow through private insurance companies and disproportionately help the largest farms, and it leaves the sugar program untouched. The SNAP extension is the benefit most widely shared with non-farm households. On balance it is a modest improvement over the 2008 law it would have replaced, not a rebalancing.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 64-35 on June 21, 2012, but when it reached the House the next week it was simply held at the desk — no hearing, no vote — and no farm bill ever came to the House floor in 2012, so the 2008 farm bill was extended instead and a new five-year law was not completed until 2014.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 24, 2012, and reported by the Senate Agriculture Committee the same day, and was immediately placed on the Senate calendar [S2][S6].
The Senate invoked cloture on the motion to proceed 90-8 on June 7, 2012, with every Democrat, independent, and 37 of 47 Republicans in favor [S7].

Two Republican motions to recommit the bill with instructions — by Senator Lee (rejected 29-70) and Senator Johnson of Wisconsin (rejected 40-59) — failed on June 20, with every Democrat voting no on both [S8][S9].
The Senate passed the amended bill 64-35 on June 21, 2012: 46 of 51 Democrats and both independents voted yes, while only 16 of 47 Republicans did [S10].
The House received the bill on June 26, 2012 and held it at the desk; the House never voted on it, and no farm bill reached the House floor that year [S6].
With the rewrite stalled, the 2008 farm bill was extended, keeping direct payments flowing, and a successor farm bill did not become law until 2014.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the interim, commodity producers kept receiving unconditional direct payments under the extension of the old law, and the crop insurance industry kept its existing arrangement; the House instead spent 2012 moving its own version, which died without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Direct-payment recipients and crop insurers, for a time

sides.party_line_note: Opening debate was near-unanimous (90-8), but final passage split sharply by party: 46 of 51 Democrats voted yes while only 16 of 47 Republicans did, and every Democrat opposed both Republican recommittal motions.

industries.note: The bill makes federally subsidized crop insurance the centerpiece of farm support: a new supplemental coverage option with 70% federal premium support, an 80% premium subsidy for the stacked income protection plan for cotton, and permanent enterprise-unit premium payments. Private insurers sell these policies and their commissions and risk-sharing arrangements scale with the subsidies taxpayers put in.

industries.industry: Producers of row crops (corn, wheat, soybeans, cotton, rice, peanuts)
industries.note: They lose unconditional direct payments, countercyclical payments, and ACRE, but gain Agriculture Risk Coverage payments at an 89% revenue guarantee, expanded insurance, and marketing loans. Their subsidy is now triggered by revenue shortfalls rather than paid every year, which is the reform, but the money still comes from taxpayers.

The dairy price support and milk income loss programs are repealed in favor of a margin protection program that pays dairies when feed-cost margins fall below $4 per hundredweight. A companion stabilization program can reduce payments to high-output dairies when margins are low, which can tighten supply and raise retail milk prices.

The bill continues nonrecourse loans to cane and beet processors at fixed rates through 2017 and suspends permanent price support authority only temporarily. In practice this program keeps domestic sugar prices above world prices, with the difference embedded in the price of food consumers buy.

SNAP is extended, guaranteeing retailers a large, reliable customer base, but participating stores must stock three categories of perishable staple foods and pay 100% of the cost of electronic benefit transfer equipment, and stores where liquor and tobacco exceed 45% of sales are excluded.
